auraIntro: Explorer, Large Magellanic Cloud is the largest satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, housing the active Tarantula Nebula.
overview: The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is a satellite galaxy orbiting the Milky Way at a distance of 160,000 light-years in the southern constellations Dorado and Mensa.
formation: Formed roughly 11 billion years ago, its irregular shape is caused by gravitational tidal forces exerted by the Milky Way.
structure: Classified as a Magellanic irregular galaxy spanning 14,000 light-years, containing a central stellar bar and roughly 20 billion stars.
discoveryHistory: Observed since antiquity by Southern Hemisphere indigenous populations; cataloged by Persian astronomer Al Sufi in 964 CE and Ferdinand Magellan in 1519.
observationTips: Prominently visible to the naked eye under dark Southern Hemisphere skies as a bright glowing cosmic cloud.
funFacts: Houses the Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus), the most energetic starburst region in the entire Local Group.
Hosted Supernova SN 1987A, the closest observed supernova explosion since Kepler's Supernova in 1604.

cards.title: Arrival: The Milky Way's Nearest Giant Satellite
cards.subtitle: Large Magellanic Cloud Overview
cards.body: Welcome to the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), the largest and brightest satellite dwarf galaxy orbiting our Milky Way. Located just 160,000 light-years away in the southern sky constellations Dorado and Mensa, the LMC spans 14,000 light-years across space and contains roughly 20 billion stars.

cards.title: Discovery: Al-Sufi to Magellan
cards.subtitle: Southern Sky Observational History
cards.body: Visible to the naked eye in the Southern Hemisphere, indigenous Australian populations observed the LMC for millennia. Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi cataloged it in 964 CE in his Book of Fixed Stars as 'Al-Bakr' (the White Ox). Ferdinand Magellan brought news of the cloud to Europe following his 1519 expedition.
bulletPoints: Cataloged by Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi in 964 CE as 'Al-Bakr'.
Documented during Ferdinand Magellan's circumnavigation voyage in 1519.
Proved to be an independent satellite galaxy by Henrietta Swan Leavitt's Cepheid period-luminosity discovery.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: The Monster Tarantula Nebula
cards.subtitle: 30 Doradus & Supernova SN 1987A
cards.body: Inside the LMC lies the Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus), the most energetic and massive starburst region in the entire Local Group. Spanning nearly 1,000 light-years across, if placed at the distance of the Orion Nebula, it would cast visible shadows on Earth. On February 23, 1987, supernova SN 1987A exploded in its outskirts.
bulletPoints: Tarantula Nebula is the largest starburst region in the Local Group.
Contains supermassive star cluster R136, holding stars over 100-200 solar masses.
SN 1987A was the closest observed supernova in modern astronomy, emitting a neutrino burst.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Webb NIRCam & MIRI Deep Scan
cards.subtitle: Resolving Thousands of Protostars
cards.body: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope imaged 30 Doradus with NIRCam and MIRI instruments. Webb's high-resolution infrared sensors penetrated dense gas pillars, revealing thousands of previously unseen young protostars, distant background galaxies, and complex hydrocarbon dust filaments.
bulletPoints: JWST infrared optics penetrate dense obscuring dust pillars in 30 Doradus.
Uncovers thousands of newly forming protostars embedded in gas clouds.
Maps fine silicate dust chemistry and radiation feedback from young massive stars.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: The Magellanic Bridge & Future Collision
cards.subtitle: Intergalactic Gas Stream & Merger Destiny
cards.body: The LMC is connected to its companion, the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), by a vast stream of gas called the Magellanic Bridge. Gravitationally bound to the Milky Way, calculations indicate that in roughly 2.4 billion years, the LMC will merge with our galaxy, driving a fresh wave of star formation across the Milky Way's disk.
bulletPoints: Connected to SMC by the Magellanic Bridge gas stream.
Milky Way's tidal forces are pulling gas out of the LMC to form the Magellanic Stream.
Expected to collide and merge with the Milky Way in approximately 2.4 billion years.
